I'm very confused by the use of "sd{a,b,c}" throughout this commit.  Aren't sdX used for the raw device and sdXN is used for partitions?  Wouldn't the boot partition be `sda0` or `sda1`?

How are we guaranteed that sda or sdb are the correct devices?  What happens if someone also plugs in a USB flash device?  Is there some kind of /sys/block identifier we could use instead?

I tested this on the AST2700 EVB. Since the UFS probe runs first, the UFS devices consistently appear as sda and sdb, even when I plug in a USB device.

If the device order does not match the expectation in some cases, I would suggest that users add a udev rule to ensure the devices are assigned stable names.
I used /dev/disk/by-path to identify the boot partition. Please help review it again. Thanks.
Done
Why?

Originally it was written as number="${number##*mmcblk0p}".
I added a rootPartition variable to make it more flexible, but that causes ShellCheck to report SC2295.
I followed the approach in [phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt](https://github.com/openbmc/phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt/blob/master/bmc/obmc-flash-bmc#L530) and added disable=SC2295 since this is a false positive.
I have rewritten it. Please help review it again. Thanks.

Yes, the by-partlabel doesn’t expose the boot partitions. For eMMC the boot partition is stable `/dev/mmcblk0boot0`, but for UFS the boot LUNs appears as `/dev/sdX`, which can change. That’s why I used by-path to find them.


Why aren't we adding a GPT for them?  This is not obvious to me.

If we don't have a GPT for them, how do we update them from Linux?

Are they stored in the MBR location?  If so, can we use the symlink from the `boot-a` to find the parent device?

I'm asking these questions because any time we start hard-coding hardware-oriented paths, it becomes wrong for one platform or another.  We have no way to know if this code is right for Nuvoton or RaspberryPI-5 or any other chip.  I'm assuming it is correct for Aspeed (2700 specifically) since you're making the contributions, but we don't want our code tied to a particular chip.  This is good even for you when you consider it might not even work on the "2800".

These are hardware partitions created external command to the device they create a unique logical sector number space.  the roms read raw content.   They are not expecting formatting and don't have code to parse partitions.  (This is similar to NVME namespaces but I don't know of anyone using those for booting yet).

On eMMC they can be updated from Linux but are provisioned by additional commands. the commands reserve a connanded number of sectors for them reducing the logical size of the main device.  I expect similar for ufs.

for Patrick's raspberry pi example the soc has a large rom that starts on the GPU and reads files from mbr marked boot partition as fat.  an open source can load from USB host, USB device, SPI, SD card, or similar.  

The question should be: is there a better way to go from the other partition back to the hardware selected by the ROM.

the difficulty is when we can choose to boot from eg removable media (SD card, USB drive, etc) with the boot started on nor instead of a hardware partition device like ufs or eMMC.  At some point this will require system specific configuration.


I think the best we can do is s start with the root and try to find the same physical device.  I agree it's a bad choice to use the sysfs pathbaw d on device tree names we already have examples of that changing over time.

@patrick@stwcx.xyz
The U-Boot boot partition isn’t described by the GPT. In obmc-flash-bmc, we need to locate that partition and update it using dd.
https://github.com/openbmc/phosphor-bmc-code-mgmt/blob/master/bmc/obmc-flash-bmc#L578-L586

```
    # Update u-boot if needed
    bootPartition="mmcblk0boot0"
    devUBoot="/dev/${bootPartition}"
    imgUBoot="${imgpath}/${version}/image-u-boot"
    if [ "$(cmp_uboot "${devUBoot}" "${imgUBoot}")" != "0" ]; then
        echo 0 > "/sys/block/${bootPartition}/force_ro"
        dd if="${imgUBoot}" of="${devUBoot}"
        echo 1 > "/sys/block/${bootPartition}/force_ro"
    fi
```

I don’t have other chip hardware right now. If we adopt those platforms and issues arise, we can keep improving this script.


@mdmii@outlook.com
eMMC exposes fixed node names like /dev/mmcblk0, /dev/mmcblk0boot0, and /dev/mmcblk0boot1. However, UFS depends on how to create UFS LUN partition. For example in U-Boot:

```
ufs create lun 0 100000 (create 16GB user area)
ufs create boot 1 1000000 (create 4MB boot part 1)
ufs create boot 2 1000000 (create 4MB boot part 2)
```

It also related [U-Boot boot command](https://github.com/AspeedTech-BMC/u-boot/blob/aspeed-master-v2023.10/include/configs/evb_ast2700.h#L29) selects the boot target and then loads the kernel via scsi. Once Linux is up, we get /dev/sdX for access.

```
ufsboota=setenv bootpart 2; setenv rootfs rofs-a; run setufsargs; ext4load scsi 0:${bootpart} ${loadaddr} fitImage && bootm ${loadaddr}; echo Error loading kernel FIT image\0" \
```

I don’t have a better way to find the boot LUN in the Linux.
